summary.text: A transform fault is a fault along a plate boundary where the plates move past each other mostly horizontally.
Because they add no lithosphere and destroy none at Earth's surface, transform boundaries are also called conservative plate boundaries.
Most lie in oceanic crust, linking offset segments of spreading ridges in a zigzag, though a few better-known ones such as the San Andreas Fault run on land.

facts.label: Fault family
facts.value: A special case of strike-slip fault

facts.label: Famous land examples
facts.value: San Andreas and North Anatolian faults

facts.label: Key insight by
facts.value: Geophysicist and geologist John Tuzo Wilson

facts.label: Prominent ocean examples
facts.value: Atlantic, between South America and Africa

items.prompt: Along a plate boundary, two plates grind sideways past each other. What happens to the amount of plate at the surface there?

options.label: New crust is added along the fault
Crust sinks and is destroyed below
None is added and none is lost
Crust piles up into new mountains

items.explain: Transform boundaries involve no addition or loss of lithosphere at the surface, which is why they are called conservative.

items.prompt: A fault joins two offset segments of a mid-ocean ridge, and an earthquake slips along it. What happens to the distance between the two ridge segments?

options.label: It grows with every earthquake
It stays the same
It shrinks a little each time
The segments soon merge into one

items.explain: Slip on a transform fault does not change the distance between the ridges it separates, because the ridges themselves are spreading centers.

items.prompt: If you mapped every fault where plates slide sideways past each other, where would you find most of them?

options.label: Deep inside the continents
Around the rims of volcanoes
Under the polar ice sheets
On the ocean floor between ridge segments

items.explain: Most transform faults are in oceanic crust, where they take up the offset between segments of divergent boundaries; fewer are on land.

items.prompt: Far from a mid-ocean ridge, a long scar on the seafloor lines up with an active sideways fault but no longer slips. What is it?

options.label: An old stretch of that fault carried off by spreading
A buried trench where a plate once dove under
A collapsed tube left by flowing lava
A canyon cut by an ancient river

items.explain: Fracture zones are former transform-fault lines that have moved past the active zone and are being pushed toward the continents.

items.prompt: Standing on one side of a sideways-slipping fault, you watch the block across from you move to your right. How is the fault classed?

options.label: Sinistral
Dextral
Normal
Reverse

items.explain: Transform faults are classed by handedness: a dextral fault has the opposite block moving right, a sinistral one has it moving left.

items.prompt: Why do ocean ridges and the faults linking them so often form a zigzag pattern?

options.label: Earthquakes slowly bend the ridge
Ocean currents erode the ridge unevenly
Spreading runs at an angle to the ridge's line
Continents push on the ridge from both sides

items.explain: The zigzag comes from oblique spreading, where the direction of motion is not perpendicular to the overall trend of the divergent boundary.
